items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: I think for Art Tatum, for Louis Armstrong, for Fats Waller, for Erroll Garner, for Clifford Brown. Hey. You know.

ctx.x: Well you mentioning Europe — and I’m only partly familiar with your story of when you were a young boy. Did you hear jazz in Austria?

Well Austria, which is where I started out, what I heard of jazz was pretty much limited, as I can tell in retrospect, from records. I liked to — my mother had a wind-up phonograph and I liked to play around with that and also her mother, my mother was one of four siblings, she was the oldest but she had two sisters and the brother. And my grandmother had a place in Upper Bavaria. It was near the Austrian border. But she had © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

bought that in 1912 to raise her family. I spent my summers there as a kid. And there were a bunch of records that belonged to my mother and her siblings, and there was dance music. But it really turns out in retrospect to have been the closest thing to real jazz was by a British trumpet player named Nat Gonella. He was an Armstrong acolyte when Louis first came to Europe — he came to England in 1932 — Nat was one of the first to welcome him and took him under his wing and got him settled in London and all that.…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It’s through Nat that I wound up meeting Louis. ... So that’s how I first got my introduction to Pops.

ctx.x: Why don’t you tell us about your ancestry, as much as you remember – your parents and even further back if you . . .

It’s a fairly complicated – but I’ll try to be brief. My father was born in what was then the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between the world wars it was Poland. After World War II it became the Soviet Union, but now it’s Ukraine. So it had a scattered history. He was born into a Hassidic family, but not in what we generally think of as eastern European Jewry. We mostly think of what they call a stetl, which is a small

town or a village. This was not even a village. It was just a collection of farmhouses, a very small spot on the map. My paternal grandfather was the manager of an estate that belonged to a Polish noblewoman. So my father grew up in a rural atmosphere. Like most Jewish kids, he went to – very early on to a school where you learn to read Hebrew. So he grew up multi­ lingual: Polish, Russian, Ukrainian. His father, unlike most Hassids, wanted him to have a formal Westernized education. He said, if you don’t know…
